Depuis l’élection de Donald Trump aux Ét: Since Donald Trump’s election in the United States, the rhetoric about immigrants has grown increasingly violent, casting them as scapegoats for many of our societies’ ills. That trend is already visible in the statements of some Quebec politicians. On the international stage, it is conflicts and other humanitarian catastrophes that cause concern.
Pour prendre un peu de hauteur sur une s: To gain some perspective on an increasingly complex situation, we invited none other than Joanne Liu, the former president of Médecins Sans Frontières, to Les Grandes Converses. We asked her about her humanitarian experience, her view of international action in the face of today’s crises, and the rise of anti-immigration rhetoric in Quebec, among other topics.
<strong>Présidente internationale de Méd: International president of Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) from 2013 to 2019, Joanne Liu, a pediatrician at Montréal’s Hôpital Sainte-Justine, is an emblematic figure of the humanitarian world. To mark the release of her book, L’Ebola, les bombes et les migrants, she answers La Converse’s questions and takes an unflinching look at Quebec, Canadian and international society. Interview.
Joanne Liu n’est pas du genre à essayer: Joanne Liu is not the type to draw attention to herself. She has devoted her life to others, first by becoming a doctor, then by committing to humanitarian work with the non-governmental organization Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF), of which she would eventually become president. True to form, she arrives quietly at the La Converse offices, where we are waiting for her along with three members of École Converse: Firas, Aya and Cindy.
Chaussures de course aux pieds, doudoune: Running shoes on her feet, puffy jacket on her back, rectangular glasses on her nose, Joanne Liu always seems ready to respond to a medical emergency. Her calm and warm smile give no hint of the tragedies, witnessed around the world, that her memory may carry.
Pédagogue, la pédiatre prête attention à: A natural teacher, the pediatrician pays attention to every word she says. You can sense – sometimes in what she doesn’t say in front of the camera, but that can be read in her book – the Quebec woman of Chinese origin, the humanitarian with a message of denunciation, the Joanne Liu who managed to carve out a place for herself in this society against all odds. She doesn’t boast about it, but she is one of the few Quebec women to have made the Time 100, the famous ranking of the world’s most influential people published every year in Time magazine.
<strong>La Converse : Vous avez récemmen: La Converse: You recently collaborated on a play titled Nos Cassandre, inspired by your life. What connection do you see between your journey and the myth of Cassandra?
<strong>‍</strong>\n<strong>Joanne Liu :: ‍ Joanne Liu: Nos Cassandre explores the idea of predicting crises without anyone listening. That’s somewhat what I experienced at Médecins Sans Frontières. During the Ebola epidemic in 2014, we warned everyone about the seriousness of the situation. We predicted that the crisis would explode if nothing was done, but unfortunately, no one took it seriously in time. That is Cassandra’s torment: seeing what is going to happen, but being unable to change the course of events.
<strong>En décembre 2024, vous avez publ: In December 2024, you published L’Ebola, les bombes et les migrants, a book in which you describe the loss of a large part of our “common humanity” in the face of global crises…
Mon propos sur l’humanité commune est de: My point about common humanity is to go back to basics: every life counts. Today, we get the impression that some lives, depending on where they are on the globe, don’t have the same value. If we don’t recognize humanity in others, we don’t recognize our own humanity. We see it clearly with migration crises and international conflicts, particularly in the Middle East. This reality compels me to urge people to see how urgent it is to preserve our common humanity.
<strong>Au sein de MSF, comment avez-vou: Within MSF, how did you handle the conflicts between humanitarian action and international politics?
Gérer les conflits entre action humanita: Handling conflicts between humanitarian action and international politics means understanding that states don’t have friends, they have interests, as Charles de Gaulle put it. When the Ebola epidemic was hitting West Africa, I noticed an icy indifference. My master’s supervisor advised me to “change the narrative.” So I reframed it: “It’s still astonishing that people are dying of a fast-moving disease, a hemorrhagic fever in West Africa, and that today the only entity capable of responding is an independent organization, and not the nations themselves.” That change in wording had the desired effect; they started thinking: “If this happened here, would we be ready?” It led to concrete action, including the setting up of laboratories where specimens could be analyzed.
<strong>Selon vous, le Canada remplit-il: In your view, is Canada fulfilling its international humanitarian obligations?
La réponse courte est non. Le Canada acc: The short answer is no. Canada puts its own citizens first, which is normal: that’s why we elect a government. However, international action often becomes a “bonus” or a secondary issue, because it doesn’t bring in votes.
Aujourd’hui, le gouvernement canadien a: Today, the Canadian government has taken a real beating. Although we are a G7 country, we are not doing everything we could do. Countries of similar size, like Norway or Oman, have been able to play a role as international mediators. Canada could have played that role in the Americas, but it would have required political courage and an investment in international diplomacy, two things that are currently lacking.
<strong>Quel regard portez-vous sur l’év: How do you view the evolution of political discourse in Quebec on the subject of immigration?
En tant qu’humanitaire, je trouve que ça: As a humanitarian, I think it has no place, having political leaders who dehumanize populations, whether they are newcomers or other communities. It’s a dangerous slide. I believe we need to rise above that. Yet these populations are portrayed as the source of all our problems: the housing crisis, problems accessing care, and even unemployment. They become the scapegoat for our malaise and are seen as a threat to our cultural identity.
La migration doit être régulée de manièr: Migration must be regulated in an orderly and humane way, as stipulated by the Global Compact for Migration, adopted in 2018. But to do that, we must be able to discuss these issues with maturity and humanity.
L’histoire montre que la déshumanisation: History shows that dehumanization is often the first step toward abuse: in Rwanda, people were called “cockroaches.” Then, once they have been dehumanized, abuses can be committed against them. Every person has a right to dignity, safety and access to care.
<strong>Certaines personnes voient l’ouv: Some people see openness to immigrants as a threat to social cohesion and to Quebec’s economy. What do you think?
Les migrants semblent, dans de nombreuse: In many regions, here as elsewhere, migrants seem to be becoming the ideal scapegoats. But this is not a new tactic: it has been done in the past with different communities.
Ce n’est pas tant des idées fausses qu’u: It’s less a matter of false ideas than a way of constructing the narrative around migrants. The numbers show that in Canada, we have never welcomed so many temporary migrants. That creates an imbalance compared with permanent migrants, but it’s not a subject that is treated neutrally.
Je crois que, lorsque des personnes se s: I believe that when people already feel they are struggling – for example, when they can’t make ends meet or feed their children properly – it becomes hard for them to show solidarity with others who arrive in precarious conditions. It’s a systemic problem.
Ce qui manque, c’est un discours imparti: What’s missing is an impartial, balanced discourse, carried by influential institutions like the media, education and politics. It is precisely the role of the media, educators, policymakers and opinion leaders to raise the level of the debate. Yet these spheres often seem to use the subject of immigration for personal or electoral capital. That prevents a real, substantive debate, and it’s deeply regrettable.
<strong>Il y a régulièrement des polémiq: Controversies regularly erupt when some people denounce a form of racial discrimination in society. Why do you think it is so hard to talk about racism in Quebec?
Je crois que cela incite à procéder à un: I think it prompts us to do some introspection, to examine whether, consciously or unconsciously, we lacked judgment at some point. Personally, as a member of a visible minority, I have faced everyday racism throughout my life. When you’re a child, for example, you have a hard time with difference. As you grow up, that discomfort can persist.
Je ne dirais pas qu’il s’agit toujours d: I wouldn’t say it’s always racism, but often a difficulty accepting difference. Today, we live in an era where difference is often perceived as confrontation, which creates discomfort. The problem is that as soon as certain terms like “systemic racism” are uttered, people bristle and tense up. That makes any open and constructive conversation almost impossible.
C’est pourquoi, de mon côté, je préfère: That’s why, for my part, I prefer to talk about tolerance rather than difference. How can we embrace that difference and include it in our collective heritage? That, in my view, is the key to a calm and enriching conversation.

<strong>Vous avez beaucoup travaillé en: You have worked extensively in Africa. How did you experience humanitarian crises as president of MSF and as a doctor?
Ebola, les attaques contre les hôpitaux: Ebola, the attacks on hospitals – like the one in Kunduz, Afghanistan – and the migration crisis changed my view of humanitarian challenges. After 9/11, for example, the obsession with security profoundly affected international solidarity. These crises taught me that there is no guidebook for dealing with them, but that MSF always finds ways to act, even in the most extreme conditions. It’s a daily learning process.
<strong>L’attaque américaine de l’hôpita: The American attack on the hospital in Kunduz, Afghanistan, in 2015 marked your term. Do you see parallels with the situation in Gaza?
L’attaque de Kunduz a été un acte totale: The Kunduz attack was a completely senseless act. The hospital was clearly identified, and its coordinates had been shared with military forces, including the United States. Yet it was bombed repeatedly, killing 42 people, including 14 of our colleagues. We had alerted the authorities, but nothing stopped the attack.
À Gaza, à l’instar de ce qui se passe en: In Gaza, as in Ukraine, hospitals continue to be targeted, and the international community still seems powerless. It’s a glaring example of the impunity enjoyed by certain powers, and of the failure to protect civilians in wartime.
<strong>Face à ces violations du droit h: Faced with these violations of humanitarian law, what is the international community doing?
Le système international est paralysé. L: The international system is paralyzed. The United Nations Security Council, because of the veto power, has become a tool of inaction. As long as the major powers aren’t directly affected, it’s hard to generate a collective response.
Mais il est crucial de continuer à dénon: But it is crucial to keep denouncing these violations and defending the principles of humanitarian law. Even if it sometimes seems pointless, we have to keep up the pressure. For example, after the Kunduz attack, we supported UN Resolution 2286 to protect humanitarian missions, but these resolutions are all too often ignored.
<strong>Vous avez aussi vécu de près la: You also experienced the Ebola crisis up close. Why was the response so slow?
Avec Ebola, l’OMS a mis beaucoup de temp: With Ebola, the WHO took a long time to recognize the emergency. The affected countries acted fairly quickly, but the international community didn’t react for several months. They had to fight alone. It was only when the virus reached the United States that things finally moved.
En revanche, pour la COVID-19, les pays: By contrast, with COVID-19, rich countries were able to quickly mobilize resources to protect their populations. This contrast shows how often the concerns of countries in the Global North dominate the management of global crises, to the detriment of the most vulnerable countries.
